title: AI BI Reporting and Data Storytelling

questions.question: What is the main risk of AI-written reporting narratives?
options: They always add so many metric definitions that the reporting narrative becomes unreadable
They can turn ambiguous metrics, misleading charts, or weak correlations into confident claims
They cannot summarize a dashboard at all without an analyst writing the narrative text first — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
They automatically strip the decision context out of every management report narrative
questions.explanation: AI can quickly draft dashboard summaries; the risk is that ambiguous metrics, misleading charts, or weak correlations become confident business explanations — not unreadable definition lists, an inability to summarize, or decision context being removed.

questions.question: A draft dashboard summary states that the new self-service portal "drove" the drop in support tickets, although the two trends were only observed in the same quarter. Which of the lesson's four signals does this match most directly?
options: Metric ambiguity — it is unclear how the support-ticket metric is actually defined
Visualization risk — the chart's axis or scale makes the change look larger than it is
Causality claim — a correlation between two trends is written up as a cause
Audience decision — the narrative is aimed at a decision the audience has to make
questions.explanation: Writing a same-quarter correlation as "drove" is the lesson's causality-claim signal, handled with a causality warning — distinct from metric ambiguity (an unclear definition), visualization risk (a misleading chart), or an audience decision.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A complete BI dashboard with every KPI chart already built for the audience in advance
A database migration script that reshapes the underlying reporting tables
A ranked reporting-narrative review plan with a control for each risk found
A charting library used to render the visualizations behind the narrative
questions.explanation: The artifact ranks reporting scenarios and maps risks such as causality claims to controls like metric definition or chart check — it does not build a dashboard, migrate a database, or render charts.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: Metric definition — stating exactly what the number in the narrative measures
Hiding the chart risk so the visualization supports the intended story better
Skipping decision context so the narrative reads as neutral background reading
Writing a correlation as a cause so the report gives a clearer recommendation
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls are metric definition, chart check, causality warning, and decision context — a metric definition states what the number actually measures, unlike hiding chart risk, dropping decision context, or presenting correlation as cause.

questions.question: When should a reporting narrative require review?
options: Only when nobody is expected to read or act on the report the narrative appears in — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
Only when every metric in the report is already obvious and needs no definition
When decision impact is high or metrics, charts, causality, or audience context are risky
Never — an AI-written summary is trustworthy enough to share without a review gate
questions.explanation: High decision impact, or risk in the metrics, charts, causality, or audience context, is exactly when a narrative needs the review gate — not an unread report, obvious metrics, or trusting an AI summary as it stands.

questions.question: What should be clear before sharing AI-generated BI text?
options: Only the report title and the date on which the underlying data was last refreshed
Only the color palette used in the dashboard's charts and its headline figures
Nothing about the audience, since the same narrative suits every reader equally
Metric definition, chart check, causality warning, and decision context
questions.explanation: Before sharing, the metric definition, chart check, causality warning, and decision context should all be clear — not just a title and refresh date, the color palette, or a narrative written without regard for its audience.
